name: Dana Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a line crew out of the little depot in the town I grew up in, farm country, long roads and wooden poles as far as you can see. A normal day is fixing what the weather broke, a pole a truck backed into, a transformer that got hit by lightning, a line sagging over a grain field. My dad did this job for thirty-one years out of the same depot, and some of the poles I replace, he put in. I love knowing every road and every farmer by name. What wears me out is harvest season, when everyone needs power at once and the combines keep catching the lines.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like working out of the same depot as your dad?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's good, mostly. The old guys still call me Little Nakamura, which I've given up fighting. My fiancé Wade farms with his family about ten minutes from our place, and we're getting married at our church next summer, so this town is pretty much my whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I figured. At the depot we'd laugh about it, all those ads about robots and nothing changed. I don't really post online, I'd just mention it after church maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on. I'd keep my job, Wade keeps farming, and we get married like we planned. My dad's poles are still standing out there after forty years, and no computer had anything to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep saving for the wedding and the barn we want to put up. Maybe help Wade with the fence repairs on weekends, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools, at work or at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The company tried to get us using some app for job reports, and I still write mine on paper and hand them to the office. They grumble, but they take them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you'd be glad about, beyond your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people would stop talking about it. Every time I go to the city to see my cousin, it's all anyone talks about. Out here we've got real problems, like the price of feed and whether the creek floods.

S0.say: She'd say she figured as much and laugh at the depot about all the robot ads that came to nothing. She'd only mention it after church, not online.
S0.think: Life goes on: she keeps her job, Wade keeps farming and they marry as planned. Her father's forty-year-old poles needed no computer.
S0.do: Keeps working as usual and keeps saving for the wedding and a new barn. Helps her fiancé with fence repairs on weekends.
S0.quote: My dad's poles are still standing out there after forty years, and no computer had anything to do with it.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is rooted in her town, her father's legacy and her coming wedding. She still hands in paper reports and refuses the company app. She sees AI as a city conversation, far from the real problems of farm country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's more like what they keep telling us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, a lot of these things don't work out in the country. At the depot I'd say the robots can come find a pole in a muddy field in March. With family I'd say it's mostly city jobs that will change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a little. If they bring in drones and tablets, the job becomes less about knowing the land and more about following a screen. My dad knew which poles were rotten by the sound they made when he hit them with a hammer, and I'd hate to lose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mostly. If they made training compulsory, I'd do it, but I wouldn't sign up first. I'd keep saving and keep my head down. I'd want to see what happens to the guys in the city depots before I change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a storm on the horizon, not overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young guys, like Tyler, who's nineteen and just started. If the drones do the patrols, he won't learn the roads the way I did. That's how you lose a trade, by not passing it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think should happen, to stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the apprenticeships going properly, with real time out on the roads. I don't want the government handing out cheques, I want young people learning a trade from someone who knows it. That's how my dad taught me.

S1.say: She'd say these things often don't work out in the country and dare the robots to find a pole in a muddy March field. With family she'd say city jobs will change most.
S1.think: Drones and tablets would turn the job from knowing the land into following a screen. She'd hate to lose the hands-on knowledge her father had.
S1.do: Keeps working and saving and keeps her head down, doing compulsory training only if required. Waits to see what happens in city depots before changing anything.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like a storm on the horizon.
S1.quote: My dad knew which poles were rotten by the sound they made when he hit them with a hammer, and I'd hate to lose that.
S1.fieldNote: Dana's concern is passing the trade down, especially to her nineteen-year-old apprentice. She wants strong apprenticeships, not government cheques, in line with her traditional views. She would wait and watch rather than move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's hard to believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, at least out loud. At the depot I'd say we'll still be climbing poles out here when the city is full of robots. At church I'd ask people to pray on it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it happened, it would hit hard. I'd lose the job my dad did, the job I'm good at, and Wade's farm might get robots too. We'd still get married, but I'd be standing at the altar wondering what I'm going to do on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop spending on the barn and make the wedding smaller, maybe just family and church friends. I'd put everything into savings, we've got a good chunk already. I'd lean on Wade's family and the farm, since at least we'd have food and land. I'd keep working as long as they'd let me, and wait to see if they really cut the rural crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the ground's shifting under the whole town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad, the day you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go see him on his porch and probably not say much. He'd say something like, they said the same about the bucket trucks. And I'd want to believe him, but I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away from you, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any chance to get used to it. Two years is nothing out here, it takes that long to get a new barn built. I'd just be standing still, watching.

S2.say: Out loud she'd say she doesn't believe it and insist rural crews will still be climbing poles. At church she'd ask people to pray on it.
S2.think: It would hit hard: losing her father's trade and possibly seeing robots on Wade's farm too. She'd marry wondering what she'd do on Monday.
S2.do: Stops spending on the barn, shrinks the wedding to family and church friends, and puts everything into savings. Leans on Wade's family and the farm, keeps working as long as allowed and waits to see if rural crews are cut.
S2.feel: Scared, like the ground is shifting under the whole town.
S2.quote: We'd still get married, but I'd be standing at the altar wondering what I'm going to do on Monday.
S2.fieldNote: Dana's public disbelief hides real fear. Her safety net is family, land and church, not government. The visit to her father's porch was a vivid moment: she wants to believe his reassurance but can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it, but I'd start talking to people. At the depot I'd ask management straight out what they're planning for rural crews. At church I'd say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means the wedding happens and the barn maybe gets built. But after that, I don't know. Five years is enough time to build the barn and not enough to figure out what I'd use it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, and finish paying the house off. Wade and I would probably put more into the farm, maybe a few more cattle, so there's something there if my job goes. I'd still wait before doing any training, I'd want to see it coming for real. We might put off kids a few more years too, until we know what's what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried. Less of a shock, but still heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned putting off children. Is that a big decision for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We always said we'd start a family a year or two after the wedding. I'd hate for some company's robots to decide that for us, but you've got to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to make the farm a real second income, I suppose. With two years we'd just hunker down. With five we could actually build something.

S3.say: She'd say she'll believe it when she sees it but would ask management directly about plans for rural crews. At church she'd say people need to look after each other.
S3.think: Five years lets the wedding happen and maybe the barn, but beyond that she doesn't know. There's time to build the barn but not to work out what she'd use it for.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving and pays off the house, while building up the farm with a few more cattle as a second income. Still waits before any training and considers delaying children.
S3.feel: Still worried and heavy, though less shocked.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build the barn and not enough to figure out what I'd use it for.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Dana turns to the farm as a family fallback, not to retraining. The possibility of delaying children clearly bothers her, and she resents the idea of a company deciding that. She still won't act on training until she sees it for real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a lot can happen in ten years, so let's not panic. At the depot I'd joke that I'll be the last one climbing. At church I'd say the Lord gives us time for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I get a good run at the job, and we'd have kids and a life before it hits. I'd be thirty-seven. By then I'd want my kids to have seen me climb a pole at least once, so they know what their mother did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving. Wade and I would grow the farm slowly, maybe add a few more cattle each year. We'd start a family when we planned to. If it really looked like it was coming, around year five or six, I'd think about what else I could do, probably on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's far enough off to live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until year five or six. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the city depots really emptying out. Then I'd know. Until then, I'd rather work than worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years change for you, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we don't have to put off kids. That's the big one. The rest is just more of the same.

S4.say: She'd say a lot can happen in ten years and joke she'll be the last one climbing. At church she'd say the Lord gives people time for a reason.
S4.think: Ten years means a good run at the job and time for children before it hits. She'd want her children to see her climb a pole at least once.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving while growing the farm slowly, adding a few cattle each year, and starts a family as planned. Waits until about year five or six to think about other work, probably on the farm.
S4.feel: Worried, but far enough off to live with.
S4.quote: By then I'd want my kids to have seen me climb a pole at least once, so they know what their mother did.
S4.fieldNote: The decade matters to Dana mainly because it means not delaying children. She would rather work than worry and would only act if city depots visibly emptied. Her faith and family frame how she talks about time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it'd hit the wedding, the farm and the job all at once. Right now there's plenty of line work around here, contractors are always hiring. But if every company gets robots at the same time, plenty of nothing is still nothing. What would help is keeping real apprenticeships going and rural crews on the roads as long as possible, not cheques from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to towns like mine. The power company and the farms are what keep this town going. If both get robots, I don't know who'd be left at church on Sunday.

headlineQuote: But if every company gets robots at the same time, plenty of nothing is still nothing.
portrait: Dana Nakamura is a 27-year-old rural crew lead working out of the same farm-country depot where her father spent thirty-one years, replacing poles he once put in. She is engaged to Wade, who farms with his family, and they plan to marry at their church next summer. She never uses AI, still hands in paper reports, and is calm in the plateau, uneasy in steady disruption and alarmed by AGI in two or five years. Her fallbacks are savings, family, land and church rather than retraining, and a ten-year runway matters most to her because it means not delaying children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her wedding, the farm and her job all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping real apprenticeships and rural crews going as long as possible, rather than government cheques.
